729.title: Sri Chand the ascetic
729.hook: Nanak's elder son chose a celibate life; the Udasi order traces itself to him
729.howItsDone: Sikhs follow the householder path the Gurus taught, and they remember Baba Sri Chand with respect as Guru Nanak's elder son and the figure the Udasi order traces itself to.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Sulakhni: the one who stayed, raising Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das while Nanak traveled. Today, the elder son's road.

A family business, three generations in. The father built it. Everyone assumes the eldest will take the keys. But the eldest's heart is somewhere else, and in the end the keys go to someone outside the family. Nobody is disowned. Families know this scene. Guru Nanak's family knew it too. Today we follow his elder son, Sri Chand, who chose a life his father didn't choose. Today's word: Udasi.
screen: `THE KEYS GO ELSEWHERE.` → `A ROAD OF HIS OWN.` → `TODAY: SRI CHAND.`

segments.voice: Sri Chand grew up while his father was out on the long road, and grew into a man drawn to stillness and renunciation. Tradition remembers him as an ascetic: celibate, living apart from the household, devoted to meditation. He never married. And the Udasis, an order of renunciants, trace themselves to him. Udasi is a word Sikhs already know from Nanak's own life, because the Guru's great journeys are called his udasis. So the son's order carries a name that echoes the father's travels. Here's the tension, and the tellings don't hide it. Guru Nanak's own way, as his hymns describe it, was the householder's way: earn honestly, share, remember God in the middle of family and work. He came home to Kartarpur, to the fields and the family. And when it came time to choose who would carry the light after him, he didn't choose either son. He chose Lehna, and named him Angad. So what do the stories know? They hold two things at once. Sikh teaching follows the householder path the Gurus walked. And tradition still remembers Sri Chand with honor, as Baba Sri Chand, the Guru's son, a man of deep devotion who took a different road. Tradition remembers later Gurus and Sri Chand meeting with respect, and Udasi teachers, it says, went on honoring Guru Nanak and singing his word. That's how respect for a different choice looks in a family of faith: you don't pretend the roads are the same, and you don't stop calling each other family.
screen: `A SON DRAWN TO STILLNESS.` · `UDASI, AN ECHO OF THE JOURNEYS.` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER'S PATH, AND ANOTHER.` · `REMEMBERED WITH HONOR.` · then, large: `A DIFFERENT PATH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone close who chose a road you didn't: a sibling who left the faith or entered it more deeply, a child who took a different city or a different kind of life. Notice the old argument that rises, and don't try to settle it; just look at them, choosing, and find one thing in their choice you can honestly honor. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with them in mind.
Udasi. The order of renunciants that traces itself to Baba Sri Chand, Guru Nanak's elder son, and a name that echoes the Guru's own journeys.
Your line: a different path. Not the same road, and still family. Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

730.title: Home to Talwandi
730.hook: tradition says his parents begged Nanak to stay; he told them his work was on the road
730.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the sakhi of Guru Nanak's return to Talwandi, his birthplace, now Nankana Sahib, as a story of love for family held together with the call to travel and teach.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Udasi: Sri Chand's road of renunciation, remembered with honor. Your line was a different path.

The airport arrivals hall. A mother on her toes behind the barrier, scanning faces. A father pretending to be calm, holding the car keys too tight. And then the one they've waited for walks through, and for a few minutes nobody can speak. Plenty of families who have sent someone far away know that hall. In the janamsakhis, Guru Nanak's parents get their arrivals hall too, on the edge of their own village. And the hardest part comes after the hug. Today: Talwandi.
screen: `THE ARRIVALS HALL.` → `A FAMILY THAT WAITED.` → `THE HARDEST PART COMES AFTER.`

segments.voice: Talwandi was the village where Nanak was born, where, tradition says, his father, Mehta Kalu, kept the village accounts, and his mother, Mata Tripta, raised him. In the tellings, after a long stretch of travel, Nanak and Mardana come back toward it. Some tellings keep a detail: Nanak doesn't walk straight in. He stops outside the village and sends Mardana ahead. Word reaches the house. His mother comes running out to find him; his father follows. Tradition says they wept, and held him, and then they begged. Stay. Rest. Take up a life here, among your people. We've waited long enough. And Nanak, in the tellings, answers with love, and doesn't move. His work, he tells them, is on the road. What does this story know? That a call can pull against the people you love most, and that the pull is real on both sides. The parents aren't villains; their begging is a natural thing. And Nanak's answer isn't coldness. The Guru Granth Sahib uses the language of family to speak of God, calling the Divine mother and father, kin and brother. A path that prays like that has not stopped honoring parents. Nanak has been called elsewhere, and he goes with his parents' tears still on his shoulder. And notice where the larger story ends up: after the journeys, Nanak settles at Kartarpur as a householder, with family around him. The road didn't swallow the home forever. But on this day at Talwandi, it had to come first.

731.title: Kauda and the oil
731.hook: tradition says a man-eating tribesman tried to boil Nanak in oil, and the oil turned cool
731.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the sakhi of Kauda to children and in katha as a story of the Guru's calm and protection, and of a feared man who was changed rather than destroyed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Talwandi: Nanak's parents begged him to stay, and he answered with love and kept to the road. Your line was called elsewhere.

Somewhere far from home, the fire is already lit. A great iron pan sits over it, full of oil, and the oil is starting to shimmer. A man named Kauda tends it. The tellings call him a man-eater, a wild and feared figure of the forest, and he has already seized Mardana. That's where this sakhi opens: not with Nanak preaching, but with Mardana in danger and the oil getting hot. The road turns frightening. Today: Kauda.
screen: `THE FIRE IS ALREADY LIT.` → `MARDANA IS SEIZED.` → `THE ROAD TURNS FRIGHTENING.`

segments.voice: In the janamsakhis, Mardana has wandered off, and Kauda catches him. Nanak comes looking, and finds his friend about to be thrown in. Tellings differ on what comes next. In the one followed here, Kauda turns on Nanak instead, seizes the Guru and drops him into the pan. And here's the wonder at the heart of it: tradition says the oil went cool. Nanak sits in it unharmed. Kauda stokes the fire, and still the oil won't burn him. And Kauda, the terror of the forest, stares, and then falls at the Guru's feet. The tellings say he changed his ways and began to remember the Name. What does this story know? Notice what Nanak doesn't do. He doesn't fight Kauda, curse him, or call down fire. The heat in the scene is all Kauda's: the fire, the pan, the hunger, the fear he spreads. And the Guru meets all that heat with a stillness so complete that it cools the oil itself. Read as a wonder, it shows the Guru's protection. Read as a picture, it shows what a calm person does to a burning room. Either way, the story ends with Kauda changed, not destroyed. We've seen that shape before on the road: the fiercest person in the story becomes a seeker by the end. Some readers see in Kauda's oil a picture of what the Guru's word can do to the fire inside a person: cool it, without destroying the person.

segments.voice: Breathe slowly and bring to mind something hot in your life right now, an argument that hasn't ended, a family chat gone sharp, without replaying it; just see the heat. Then let your breath go slower, and ask what the coolest thing you could bring to it would be: not winning, not silence, maybe a softer first sentence. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you breathe out.

Your line: the oil went cool. Stillness met the heat, and no one was destroyed. Until tomorrow.

732.title: The land of the enchantresses
732.hook: tradition says Mardana was bewitched in a far country and Nanak's singing set him free
732.howItsDone: Sikhs gather in gurdwaras for kirtan, singing the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib together, and tell this sakhi as a picture of the Guru's word breaking the spells of maya.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kauda: the feared man whose oil, tradition says, went cool, and who ended changed, not destroyed. Your line was the oil went cool.

A song comes on in a shop, and the man at the till starts humming without noticing. Hours later, at home, the tune is still with him. A friend hums a grandmother's lullaby, and a grown woman is suddenly six years old. Songs get into people in ways arguments rarely do. The janamsakhis knew that. Mardana, the Guru's companion, was a musician, and in today's sakhi he gets into trouble in a far country, the kind no argument can get him out of.
screen: `A SONG IN A SHOP.` → `SONGS GET IN WHERE ARGUMENTS DON'T.` → `MARDANA IN A FAR COUNTRY.`

segments.voice: In the tellings, Nanak and Mardana come to a country ruled by women, a land famous for magic. Mardana, hungry, goes ahead to find food, and doesn't come back. A woman there has cast a spell on him. Some tellings say she turned him into a ram, tied up with a thread. Others simply say he lost himself, forgot who he was and why he'd come. Nanak goes looking, and finds his friend bound and bewildered. And the Guru doesn't argue with the spell. He sings. Tradition says the sound of the Guru's hymn broke the enchantment, and Mardana came back to himself. Then the women of that land try their arts on Nanak: charms, threads, spells, and in some tellings riches and beauty offered by their queen. None of it holds him. He keeps singing. And the tellings end with the enchantresses listening, and changed. So what does this story know? Some hear a plain wonder: the Guru's power over magic. Some readers also hear quieter spells in it: the pull of wanting, of distraction, of forgetting who you are. The Gurus' hymns have a name for that pull: maya. And the story's answer isn't a lecture. It's kirtan, the singing of the Guru's word, the same singing that fills a gurdwara today. Mardana's own instrument, the rabab, sits at the beginning of that song.
screen: `A COUNTRY FAMOUS FOR MAGIC.` · `MARDANA LOSES HIMSELF.` · `THE GURU SINGS, THE SPELL BREAKS.` · `KIRTAN, ANSWER TO MAYA.` · then, large: `SINGING SETS FREE.`

segments.voice: Let a song come to mind, a hymn if you have one, a lullaby, any tune that once brought you back to yourself, and hum it under your breath or just hear it inside. Then think of someone who seems stuck today under some spell of gloom or worry, and hold them in the tune for a while. If you pray, you can let the tune carry Waheguru.
Kirtan, the Guru's singing that, in the sakhi, broke the spell on Mardana in a far country and set him free.
Your line: singing sets free. A song gets in where arguments don't. Day seven hundred thirty-two, done.

733.title: The bitter fruit made sweet
733.hook: tradition says a hungry Mardana ate bitter soapnuts at Nanak's word and found them sweet
733.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the reetha sakhi as a story of trust and gratitude, and tradition links a gurdwara in the hills, named for the reetha tree, to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan: the Guru sang, and the spell on Mardana broke. Your line was singing sets free.

Soapnuts. Some people still use them for laundry: small brown shells, dropped into a cloth bag and tossed in the wash, and they foam like soap. They aren't food. They're bitter enough to make a whole face fold up. Hold on to that, because in today's sakhi, a starving man is told to eat them. Mardana is in the hills, hungry again, and the only food in sight grows on the wrong tree. Today: reetha.
screen: `SOAPNUTS: FOR LAUNDRY.` → `BITTER ENOUGH TO FOLD A FACE.` → `A HUNGRY MAN, THE WRONG TREE.`

segments.voice: In the tellings, Nanak and Mardana are walking through wild hill country, far from any village. Mardana is hungry, and says so, the way he does more than once in these stories. He's the very human one on the road, the one who gets tired and wants his dinner. Nanak points to a tree: a reetha, a soapnut tree. Eat, he says. Mardana hesitates. Soapnuts are bitter, and he knows it. But he trusts the Guru, picks one, and bites. And tradition says it was sweet, sweet enough to fill him. Tradition links a gurdwara in those hills to this story, and it carries the tree's name. What does the story know? Something about hunger and about trust. Mardana doesn't get a feast. He gets the plain thing in front of him, the thing he'd have walked past, and it's the Guru's word that changes the taste. The Gurus' hymns speak of the Name as sweet. They speak of accepting what comes as the sweet will of God. So the sakhi turns that teaching into fruit. However the wonder is held, the scene makes a plain point: the same bite can taste bitter or sweet depending on what's brought to it. Met with complaint, it's soap. Received with thanks, in the Guru's name, it fed a hungry man. The sakhi doesn't ask Mardana to pretend the fruit isn't bitter. It asks him to take one bite.

segments.voice: Take one plain thing if you have it nearby, a piece of bread, a cracker, a glass of water, or simply remember the last plain thing you ate. Taste it slowly, notice the taste before you judge it, and give thanks for it, out loud or inside, as if it were the best thing on the table. If you pray, you can say Waheguru before the first bite.

734.title: The yogis' seat
734.hook: tradition says the Gorakhnath yogis' center later took Nanak's name, Nanakmata
734.howItsDone: Sikhs visit Gurdwara Nanakmata Sahib as a place of pilgrimage and tell the sakhi of the yogis' seat and the pipal tree that turned green.

segments.voice: Yesterday, reetha: the bitter soapnut Mardana ate at the Guru's word, and tradition says it was sweet. Your line was bitter made sweet.

A campsite sign: leave it better than you found it. A rental apartment with a note on the fridge from the last guests, thanking whoever comes next. Some places even take the name of a visitor who changed them. That's today's sakhi. The road has carried Guru Nanak and Mardana through oil and enchantment and bitter fruit. Now it brings them to a seat that belonged to someone else, a center of yogis, and a place that would one day carry a new name. Today: Gorakhmata.
screen: `LEAVE IT BETTER THAN YOU FOUND IT.` → `A PLACE TAKES A VISITOR'S NAME.` → `A SEAT THAT BELONGED TO OTHERS.`

segments.voice: The yogis in this story followed Gorakhnath, the teacher their order looks back to, and their center in the foothills was known by his name, Gorakhmata. We've met Gorakhnath's yogis before this year, on the mountain and at Achal, asking Nanak hard questions. Here, tradition says, the Guru comes to their own home ground and sits down under a dry, dead pipal tree. And the tree turns green. The yogis are not pleased to find a stranger on their seat. The tellings show them trying their powers to move him, and failing, and then sitting down to talk. And some of them stay to listen. In time, tradition says, the place itself took the Guru's name: Nanakmata. A gurdwara stands there now, and Sikhs go there as pilgrims. Here's what the story knows. Nanak doesn't take the yogis' seat by force, and he doesn't tear anything down. The dead tree comes back to life where he sits. The story doesn't mock the yogis; Guru Nanak treated them as serious seekers, worth arguing with because they were in earnest. His hymns ask them to carry their discipline inward, to make contentment their earrings and the Name their practice. That's a visitor who leaves a place better: not by erasing what was there, but by making something grow where he sat.

735.title: Cooking at the eclipse
735.hook: at Kurukshetra Nanak cooked food on an eclipse day, and tradition says he answered the objections with a hymn
735.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the Kurukshetra sakhi as an example of Guru Nanak questioning rituals by asking what they are for, and Sikh teaching places inner truth above outward observance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gorakhmata: a dead tree turned green where Nanak sat, and the place came to carry his name. Your line was leave it better.

A huge crowd at a holy place. Pilgrims have come from far and wide to bathe and pray, on a day when the sun is about to go dark. Everyone is waiting, watching the sky. And in the middle of it all, a traveler lights a cooking fire. Today: Kurukshetra.
screen: `PILGRIMS AT A HOLY PLACE.` → `A CROWD, A DARKENING SUN.` → `A TRAVELER LIGHTS A FIRE.`

segments.voice: The place was Kurukshetra, a holy site where pilgrims gathered on the day of a solar eclipse to bathe and pray. The custom there held that no food should be cooked while the eclipse lasted. In the tellings, Guru Nanak and Mardana arrive, set up camp near the crowd, and Nanak starts a fire and begins to cook. Some tellings say the food was meat, given to him by a visitor. Smoke rises. People notice. Priests and pilgrims gather, upset, and the argument begins: why would anyone cook on this of all days? Tradition says the Guru answered not with a lecture but with a hymn. The Guru Granth Sahib holds a hymn that tradition links to this moment. In paraphrase, it says that fools quarrel over flesh, but understand nothing of wisdom or meditation. Some readers hear it turning the question away from what's on the fire and toward what's in the heart. Now notice how Nanak questions the custom. He doesn't shout from a distance or mock people at prayer. He does one small, visible thing, lets it raise the question, and then sings. The crowd comes to him, curious and angry, and leaves with something to think about. We've seen this before on his road. He questioned rituals he thought had lost their meaning, in more than one tradition, and he did it by asking what a practice is for. Sikh teaching carries that on: what matters is the inner truth a custom points to. Today's story isn't a verdict on the pilgrims. It's a picture of how to question kindly, in the middle of a crowd.
screen: `KURUKSHETRA, AN ECLIPSE DAY.` · `A COOKING FIRE IN THE CROWD.` · `THE ANSWER IS A HYMN.` · `ASK WHAT A PRACTICE IS FOR.` · then, large: `KINDLY, QUESTION IT.`

segments.voice: Find one small habit of your own that you keep without knowing why, a lucky shirt, knocking on wood, not saying a hope out loud in case it breaks, and don't sneer at it. Ask it gently what it's for, what it's trying to protect, and whether there's a truer way to protect that. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you ask.
Kurukshetra, the holy site where Nanak lit a cooking fire on an eclipse day, and tradition says he answered the objections with a hymn.
Your line: kindly, question it. With curiosity, never with scorn. A week on the road, done.
